children: If the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield remains above 5%, millions of people who rely on stock-generated income to pay their living expenses could grow worried. But fret not-the options market offers a way out  The effects are already being felt. The ProShares S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats exchange-traded fund is down about 3% since the 10-year Treasury closed above 5% on Sept. 15 for the first time since 2007. The State Street Utilities Sector SPDR ETF, also favored by dividend seekers, has lost 4% over the same period.

A deeper decline in the stocks is possible if the Federal Reserve increases interest rates again, as is expected. Higher bond yields could alarm retirees with low thresholds for market volatility and an overreliance on dividends. Dividend stocks are highly sensitive to interest rates because they tend to offer payouts that rival bonds. When bond returns increase, dividend stocks tend to decline, as they look less attractive.

Dividends might remain stable, but investors could panic when they see the value of their portfolio fall-and companies could cut dividends, or limit increases, as a rising-rate environment increases debt expenses.

The utility sector, for its part, has attracted enormous trading interest-and it doesn't seem to bode well. Bearish short selling on the Utilities ETF was the most active in about six years, per Goldman Sachs data, even as upside call option buying was recently at the highest levels in a year. While some traders point to the call activity as a bet on an XLU rebound, or a short squeeze, our read is that investors short XLU bought calls-which increase in value when stock prices rise-to hedge their bets.

Too few Americans have enough saved for retirement. They have been forced to own more stocks than recommended for their age to maintain their standard of living. They have high portfolio risk at a stage of life that historically was defined by conservative, bond-heavy portfolios.

If yields keep rising, bonds will become competitive with stocks and millions of retirees could see something that has rarely occurred in the past 30 years: the failure of stock prices to snap higher after a decline in value. Many will likely sell equities if they can finally get higher, and safer, bond returns.
Aggressive investors can wager against the Dividend Aristocrat ETF, which, at $54.60, is below its 20-day simple moving average of $56.15-a fact that attracts bearish traders like sharks to chum.

With the ETF at current levels, buy the November $54 put and sell the November $48 put to profit from a decline. The trade generates a credit of about $1.75, but trading volumes are light. At $48, the put spread-buying one put and selling another with a lower strike price but the same expiration-is worth a maximum profit of $7.75.
Dividend-reliant investors, for their part, can buttress their positions by selling calls on stocks, which creates what we call "conditional dividends" that often exceed common stock dividends.

With the State Street Utilities ETF at $39.72, the December $42 call could be sold for about 65 cents. If the stock is below $42 at expiration, the call premium is kept. XLU yields about 3%, and it pays an annual dividend of $1.21. The strategy risk is if XLU exceeds the strike price, requiring investors to buy the call at a loss, or to adjust it to avoid assignment.

Take note: Options income is taxed at personal income rates when generated by a short-term options strategy. Qualified dividend income is taxed at an attractive 15% rate. In addition, selling a call obligates an investor to sell stock if the stock price exceeds the strike price. To avoid that, the call can be adjusted, or rolled, to another expiration.
A proactive approach seems smart since dividend stock tremors could worsen, prompting investors to seek the relative safety of bonds over the multifactorial risks of stocks.
